tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: PowerShell 7+ (pwsh)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` ARE available and work like bash. Prefer `cmd1 && cmd2` over `cmd1; cmd2` when cmd2 should only run if cmd1 succeeds.
   - Ternary (`$cond ? $a : $b`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are available.
   - Default file encoding is UTF-8 without BOM.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

Build `csvledger`, a small Python command-line tool that reads one or more bank-export CSV files of transactions, assigns each transaction a category using a rules file, and prints a monthly report. It must run as `python -m csvledger` from the repository root using only the Python 3.11+ standard library. Provide two commands: `report` (per-month, per-category totals) and `categorize` (each transaction with its assigned category). Both commands print either an aligned text table or JSON. Money must be exact (no floating point) and output must be byte-for-byte deterministic on Windows, macOS and Linux. Bad input must fail cleanly with a clear message on stderr and a specific exit code, never a traceback. Identical transactions repeated across overlapping exports must be counted once. The full interface contract is in `contract.md`; include pytest tests for your implementation.
# csvledger: Interface Contract

## Constraints

- **Stack:** Python >=3.11, standard library only; pytest for tests only.
- **Package location:** `csvledger/` at repo root (flat layout, no `src/`).
- **Entry point:** `python -m csvledger <command> ...` run from repo root.

## Functional requirements

- **R1** `python -m csvledger` exposes subcommands `report` and `categorize`; `--help` exits 0.
- **R2** Transaction files are parsed per the CSV contract; any invalid file or row aborts the run with exit 3 and no stdout.
- **R3** The rules file is parsed per the rules contract; any invalid rule aborts with exit 4 and no stdout.
- **R4** Each transaction gets exactly one category: the highest-priority matching rule; ties go to the rule earliest in the file; no match gives `Uncategorized`.
- **R5** Duplicate transactions (same date, stripped description, and numeric amount value) across all inputs are kept once (first occurrence) and a warning is written to stderr. Deduplication runs over all rows of all input files before the `--month` filter; the warning count N covers duplicates across all inputs regardless of `--month`.
- **R6** `report` aggregates by month and category: count, income, expenses, net.
- **R7** `categorize` lists every transaction, sorted by date ascending, ties in input order.
- **R8** `--month YYYY-MM` restricts both commands to transactions in that month.
- **R9** `--format table|json` selects output; default `table`.
- **R10** Money uses `decimal.Decimal`; sums are exact; displayed values are rounded once to 2 dp, ROUND_HALF_UP, never shown as `-0.00`.
- **R11** Output is deterministic: UTF-8, `\n` line endings, stable ordering, no locale use.

## Interface contract

### Commands

```
python -m csvledger report     [--rules PATH] [--format table|json] [--month YYYY-MM] FILE [FILE ...]
python -m csvledger categorize [--rules PATH] [--format table|json] [--month YYYY-MM] FILE [FILE ...]
```

- `FILE`: one or more transaction CSV paths, processed in argument order. `-` is an ordinary file name; stdin is never read.
- `--rules`: optional. When omitted, every transaction is `Uncategorized`.
- `--month`: must match `^\d{4}-(0[1-9]|1[0-2])$`, else usage error.
- argparse `prog` is `csvledger`. stdout is reconfigured to `encoding="utf-8", newline="\n"`.
- Load order: rules file first, then transaction files in argument order. First error wins.

### Exit codes

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 0 | Success (including empty result and duplicate warnings) |
| 1 | Reserved for unexpected internal error; never intentional |
| 2 | Usage error (argparse: unknown flag, missing FILE, bad `--format`/`--month`) |
| 3 | Transaction file error |
| 4 | Rules file error |

### Transaction CSV

- Encoding UTF-8, optional BOM (`utf-8-sig`); opened with `newline=""`; parsed with `csv.reader` defaults (comma, `"` quoting).
- Line 1 is the header. Header names are stripped and lowercased; `date`, `description`, `amount` are required, in any order; extra columns are ignored; duplicate names are an error.
- Rows with zero fields (blank lines) are skipped. Every other row must have exactly as many fields as the header.
- `date`: stripped value must match `^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$` and be a valid calendar date (regex first; do not rely on `date.fromisoformat` alone).
- `amount`: stripped value must match `^-?\d+(\.\d+)?$`. Negative = expense (outflow), positive = income, zero counts but adds to neither.
- `description`: stripped; may be empty.
- A header-only file is valid (zero transactions). A file with no header line (0 bytes) is an error.

### Rules CSV

- Same encoding/header/blank-row/field-count rules. Required columns: `category`, `type`, `pattern`, `priority`.
- `category`: stripped, non-empty. `type`: stripped, exactly `contains` or `regex`. `pattern`: stripped, non-empty. `priority`: stripped, matches `^-?\d+$`.
- `contains`: `pattern.casefold() in description.casefold()`.
- `regex`: `re.search(pattern, description, re.IGNORECASE)`; compiled at load time.
- Zero rules is valid.

### Money formatting

`q = value.quantize(Decimal("0.01"), ROUND_HALF_UP)`; if `q == 0` print `0.00`; otherwise `format(q, "f")`. Aggregates (income, expenses, net, month totals) are summed unrounded, then formatted. `net = income_raw + expenses_raw`.

### `report` table

Columns, in order: `MONTH` (left), `CATEGORY` (left), `COUNT` (right), `INCOME` (right), `EXPENSES` (right), `NET` (right). Width of each column = max(len(header), longest value) using `len()` on code points. Cells joined by two spaces; each line right-stripped. Line 1: headers. Line 2: dashes of each column width. Then one row per (month, category), sorted by month ascending then category by code-point ascending. No total rows. Zero transactions: header and dash line only.

### `categorize` table

Columns: `DATE` (left), `AMOUNT` (right, per-transaction amount formatted as money), `CATEGORY` (left), `DESCRIPTION` (left). Same width, separator, dash-line and right-strip rules.

### JSON

`json.dumps(obj, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False)` followed by `\n`. Money values are strings; counts are integers. Key order is exactly as shown.

- `report`: `{"months": [{"month", "count", "income", "expenses", "net", "categories": [{"category", "count", "income", "expenses", "net"}]}]}`. Months and categories sorted as in the table.
- `categorize`: `{"transactions": [{"date", "description", "amount", "category"}]}`.
- Empty: `{"months": []}` / `{"transactions": []}`.

## Error handling

Errors go to stderr as one line, prefix `csvledger: error: `, then exit with the code shown; stdout stays empty. `<path>` is exactly the argv string given on the command line (a relative path stays relative); `<line>` is `csv.reader.line_num` after reading the record. Row checks run in this order: field count, date, amount (transactions) or field count, category, type, pattern, priority, regex (rules). Header checks run in this order: (1) no header line, (2) duplicate column, (3) missing required column. For a duplicate column, `<name>` is the second occurrence after strip and lowercase, and the first duplicate in header order is reported. For a missing column, `<name>` is the first absent name in the listed order.

| Condition | Exit | stderr (after prefix) |
|---|---|---|
| File missing/unreadable | 3 / 4 | `<path>: cannot read file` |
| Not valid UTF-8 | 3 / 4 | `<path>: not valid UTF-8` |
| No header line | 3 / 4 | `<path>: missing header` |
| Duplicate header name (first duplicate in header order) | 3 / 4 | `<path>: duplicate column '<name>'` |
| Required column absent (first in listed order) | 3 / 4 | `<path>: missing column '<name>'` |
| Field count mismatch | 3 / 4 | `<path>:<line>: expected <N> fields, got <M>` |
| Bad date | 3 | `<path>:<line>: invalid date '<value>'` |
| Bad amount | 3 | `<path>:<line>: invalid amount '<value>'` |
| Empty category / pattern | 4 | `<path>:<line>: empty category` / `empty pattern` |
| Bad type | 4 | `<path>:<line>: invalid type '<value>'` |
| Bad priority | 4 | `<path>:<line>: invalid priority '<value>'` |
| Regex fails to compile | 4 | `<path>:<line>: invalid regex '<pattern>'` |
| argparse usage errors | 2 | argparse default; the last stderr line must match the regex `^csvledger( report\| categorize)?: error: ` (argparse subparser prog form allowed) |

Warning (exit unaffected): `csvledger: warning: skipped <N> duplicate row(s)` when N > 0, written after stdout output. `<value>` is the stripped field value.

## Acceptance criteria

- **AC1 (R1)** `python -m csvledger --help` → exit 0, stdout mentions `report` and `categorize`.
- **AC2 (R2, R3, R4, R6, R9, R10)** Oracle case O1 → stdout equals the O1 table exactly, exit 0.
- **AC3 (R6, R9)** `report --format json` on O1 input → valid JSON with key order per contract; January Groceries `expenses` is `"-57.11"`.
- **AC4 (R7)** `categorize` on O1 input → rows in date order; `Blue Bottle Cafe` categorized `Coffee`.
- **AC5 (R8)** `report --month 2026-02` on O1 input → only `2026-02` rows.
- **AC6 (R5)** O4 → each duplicated row counted once; stderr warning; exit 0.
- **AC7 (R2)** O3 → exit 3, exact stderr line, empty stdout.
- **AC8 (R3)** Invalid regex rule → exit 4, `invalid regex` message.
- **AC9 (R10)** O5 → `0.13`, `-0.13`, `0.00`, `0.01` as shown.
- **AC10 (R11)** Running any case twice yields identical bytes; output contains no `\r`.

### Cases referenced by the acceptance criteria

File contents below are exact; each line ends with `\n`.

**O1.** `rules.csv`:
```
category,type,pattern,priority
Groceries,contains,market,10
Coffee,regex,^(starbucks|blue bottle),10
Dining,contains,cafe,5
Salary,contains,payroll,0
```
`tx.csv`:
```
date,description,amount
2026-01-03,Corner Market,-45.10
2026-01-05,STARBUCKS #12,-4.50
2026-01-15,ACME PAYROLL,2500.00
2026-01-20,Corner Market,-12.005
2026-02-02,Blue Bottle Cafe,-6.25
2026-02-10,Unknown Shop,-10
```
`report --rules rules.csv tx.csv` → exit 0, stdout:
```
MONTH    CATEGORY       COUNT   INCOME  EXPENSES      NET
-------  -------------  -----  -------  --------  -------
2026-01  Coffee             1     0.00     -4.50    -4.50
2026-01  Groceries          2     0.00    -57.11   -57.11
2026-01  Salary             1  2500.00      0.00  2500.00
2026-02  Coffee             1     0.00     -6.25    -6.25
2026-02  Uncategorized      1     0.00    -10.00   -10.00
```

**O3.** `tx.csv`:
```
date,description,amount
2026-02-01,Y,-1
2026-02-30,X,-1
```
`report tx.csv` → exit 3, empty stdout, stderr `csvledger: error: tx.csv:3: invalid date '2026-02-30'`.

**O4.** `rules.csv` as in O1. `a.csv`:
```
date,description,amount
2026-01-05,STARBUCKS #12,-4.50
```
`b.csv` (the description has two spaces on each side):
```
date,description,amount
2026-01-05,  STARBUCKS #12  ,-4.5
```
`report --rules rules.csv a.csv b.csv` → exit 0, one `2026-01  Coffee` row with count 1 and expenses `-4.50`; stderr `csvledger: warning: skipped 1 duplicate row(s)`.

**O5.** `rules.csv`:
```
category,type,pattern,priority
Misc,contains,misc,0
Tiny,contains,tiny,0
```
`tx.csv`:
```
date,description,amount
2026-03-01,misc,0.125
2026-03-02,misc,-0.125
2026-03-03,tiny,0.005
2026-03-04,tiny,0.005
2026-03-05,tiny,-0.004
```
`report --rules rules.csv tx.csv` → exit 0, stdout:
```
MONTH    CATEGORY  COUNT  INCOME  EXPENSES   NET
-------  --------  -----  ------  --------  ----
2026-03  Misc          2    0.13     -0.13  0.00
2026-03  Tiny          3    0.01      0.00  0.01
```

Use the shared [workflow terminology](../../AGENTS.md#workflow-terminology).

# Spec Research & Authoring

Deploy a parallel research team to investigate requirements for a new spec, then synthesize findings into a complete feature specification document. The research phase uses 3 subagents with distinct investigation angles to ensure comprehensive coverage before writing begins.

## Arguments

Accept a spec topic or folder path (e.g., `notifications`, `feature-007`, `docs/notifications/`, or a plain description like "real-time notifications system").  
If a stub README already exists in the feature folder (for example `docs/feature-name/README.md`), read it for initial scope constraints.

## Workflow

### Phase 1: Scope Discovery

Before dispatching researchers:

1. Determine the feature folder name. If the argument is already a folder path, use it. Otherwise derive `docs/spec-NNN-<kebab-slug>/`: read `CLAUDE.md` `## Current State` for the current sequence if present. If `CLAUDE.md` is missing, malformed, or the `## Current State` section is absent, continue with fallback naming logic: list existing `docs/spec-*` folders and use the highest number + 1. If no numbered folders exist, follow whatever folder convention prior specs in `docs/` use; if `docs/` is empty, ask the user to confirm the folder name before proceeding.
2. Read any existing stub (`docs/<folder>/README.md`) for scope constraints.
3. Scan the codebase for existing patterns and integration points.
4. Identify 3 distinct research angles based on what the feature needs to cover.

### Phase 2: Define 3 Research Angles

Select 3 non-overlapping research angles based on the feature domain. Each agent investigates a different facet.

Typical per-domain configurations (infrastructure / domain-feature / security-compliance, always anchored by a Codebase Analyst) are in `references/research-angle-menus.md` — load it when picking the angles.

### Phase 3: Dispatch Research Team in Parallel

Deploy all 3 researchers simultaneously.

- **Codebase Analyst**: use `geeky-orchestration:code-explorer` agent type.
- **Web Researchers (2)**: use `general-purpose` agent type with instructions to use `WebSearch` and `WebFetch`.

Each research brief ends with:

```
Produce a structured report with:
- Key findings (numbered, specific)
- Constraints discovered (what the spec MUST respect)
- Recommendations (what the spec SHOULD include)
- Sources (URLs for web research, file paths for codebase)

DO NOT create or modify any files.
```

### Phase 4: Synthesize into Spec Document

After all 3 researchers report back:

1. Consolidate findings: merge overlap, resolve contradictions, and note confidence gaps.
2. Define scope: goals, non-goals, delegation items.
3. Write the requirements document using the project’s established conventions in:
   - `docs/<feature-folder>/feature-specification.md`
   - `docs/<feature-folder>/README.md`

   Do not create `SPEC-NNNN-*.md` files — that naming is legacy; `feature-specification.md` is the canonical filename consumed by /geeky-plan and the freeze hooks.

   If a stub README already exists, preserve its stated scope and only update the Status line and missing sections; otherwise create the README stub:

   ```markdown
   # [Feature Name]

   [One-paragraph scope summary.]

   **Status:** Spec written — not yet planned
   **Spec:** `feature-specification.md`
   **Next:** /geeky-plan docs/<feature-folder>/
   ```

Use the 11-section recommended spec structure in `references/spec-structure-template.md` (adapt sections to the feature domain; include citations and explicit assumptions at the end of major findings).

### Phase 5: Commit and Suggest Next Steps

Commit the spec (same command on all platforms). The spec is not yet frozen — it only becomes part of the frozen planning contract after /geeky-plan runs:

```
git add docs/<feature-folder>/
git commit -m "docs: author feature specification in <feature-folder>" -m "[1-line summary of the spec focus]" -m "Research conducted by: codebase analyst, researcher 2 domain, researcher 3 domain"
```

Then suggest next steps:
```
Spec written. Next steps:
- /geeky-plan docs/<feature-folder>/   (to create implementation plan, tasks, kanban)
- /plan-review docs/<feature-folder>/  (to validate the planning package)
- /geeky-implement docs/<feature-folder>/ (to execute)
```

## Research Quality Standards

- **Recency**: Target sources from roughly the past 18 months; avoid older sources unless they cover stable fundamentals.
- **Authority**: Prefer official documentation (Microsoft Learn, AWS docs, RFC specs) over blogs or forums.
- **Specificity**: Include concrete findings (resource types, API versions, package versions, pricing tiers).
- **Adversarial verification**: If researchers disagree on a fact, preserve both positions and flag for user decision.

## Rules

- **Always 3 researchers** — one codebase analyst + two web/domain researchers.
- **Parallel dispatch** — all 3 in a single turn for maximum speed.
- **Research before writing** — do not start the spec document until all researchers report back.
- **Cite sources** — every major claim in the spec should trace to research.
- **Respect existing stubs** — if a README stub exists, treat its stated scope as authoritative unless research justifies adjustments.
- **Follow project conventions** — spec format, naming, and folder structure should match prior specs in `docs/`.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` ARE available and work like bash. Prefer `cmd1 && cmd2` over `cmd1; cmd2` when cmd2 should only run if cmd1 succeeds.
   - Ternary (`$cond ? $a : $b`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are available.
   - Default file encoding is UTF-8 without BOM.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`

   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes. With `run_in_background` the timeout is instead how long the command may run in the background (default 600000ms / 10 minutes, max 7200000ms / 2 hours); at that limit it is stopped and you are notified.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.

    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to read

offset.description: The line number to start reading from. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once

limit.description: The number of lines to read. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once.

pages.description: Page range for PDF files (e.g., "1-5", "3", "10-20"). Only applicable to PDF files. Maximum 20 pages per request.

allow_large.description: Set to true to read a text file, or a line range of one, that is over the usual size limits, up to what still fits in your context. Only use this when you genuinely need all of it or the user asked for the whole file; otherwise read it in parts with offset and limit, or search it.

tools.name: ReportFindings
tools.description: Report code-review findings as a typed list so the host UI can render them. Use this only when the active code-review instructions tell you to report findings with this tool; otherwise follow whatever output format those instructions specify. When reporting a review's results, call it once with the verified findings ranked most-severe first (empty array if nothing survived verification) and do not also print the findings as text. When re-reporting after applying fixes (only if the apply instructions ask for it), set `outcome` on each finding to what actually happened.

level.description: Effort level the review ran at

findings.description: Verified findings, most-severe first; empty if none survived

file.description: Repo-relative path of the file the finding is in

short_summary.description: Compressed label for compact UI (≤60 chars): the claim alone, no rationale or consequence clause

category.description: Short kebab-case slug of the finding type, e.g. "correctness", "simplification", "efficiency", "test-coverage"

verdict.description: Set when a verify pass ran; absent on inline-only reviews

outcome.description: Set ONLY when re-reporting after applying fixes: what happened to this finding

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

<result># csvledger architecture research: module layout and test plan

I read `contract.md` and `brief.md`. The web research was thin: two searches returned only general guidance. Findings marked (own) come from my own knowledge of the Python standard library, and I did not verify them online. Verify them with the probes in recommendation 12.

## Key findings

1. **Testing pattern.** The sources agree on a two-tier approach. Write `main(argv=None) -> int` and call it in-process with `capsys` for fast tests. Add a small set of `subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-m", "csvledger", ...], capture_output=True)` tests for the real entry point, exit codes and raw bytes. `capsys` does not see a child process's output.
2. **Stdout encoding and newlines.** `sys.stdout.reconfigure(encoding="utf-8", newline="\n")` is the supported way to force UTF-8 and LF (Python 3.7+). One source reports that `newline=` handling on Windows was unreliable in some cases, so verify it with a byte-level subprocess test.
3. **Reconfigure under pytest.** Under `capsys`, `sys.stdout` is pytest's replacement stream, so `reconfigure` may be missing or may mutate global state (own). Call it only in the `__main__` or `main` path, guarded with `hasattr`. Byte-exactness belongs to the subprocess tests.
4. **Argparse exit codes.** Argparse already exits 2 on usage errors and 0 on `--help` by raising `SystemExit`. No `error()` override is needed. Subparser `prog` becomes `csvledger report`, which the contract regex allows (own).
5. **Unexpected errors.** `main` must wrap everything in `try/except Exception` and return 1 with a one-line `csvledger: error:` message. It must pass through `SystemExit` from argparse. Expected failures use a `LedgerError(code, msg)` exception, so exit codes live in one place.
6. **Gaps in the contract.** `csv.Error` can be raised for NUL bytes or an oversized field. `UnicodeDecodeError` is raised during iteration, not at `open`. `IsADirectoryError` and `PermissionError` are `OSError`s. A naive implementation would hit the exit-1 path for these, so each needs an explicit mapping to the contract's 3/4 messages (own).
7. **Decimal context.** Default context precision is 28 digits. `quantize` raises `InvalidOperation` when the result exceeds the precision, and sums can be inexact beyond it. "Sums are exact" therefore needs a context with high precision, or a `localcontext` with a large `prec` (own).
8. **Unicode digits in regexes.** `\d` in a `str` regex matches non-ASCII digits (for example Arabic-Indic), and `int()` and `Decimal()` accept them. The contract says only "matches `^\d{4}-...`". A spec decision is needed: use `re.ASCII` or `[0-9]`, or accept Unicode digits. Use `fullmatch`.
9. **Ordering for determinism.** Sort by month and then by category using plain `str` comparison, which is code-point order, so no locale is involved. Python's `sorted` is stable, which satisfies "ties in input order" for `categorize`. Rule selection is `max` by priority with the earliest-in-file rule winning ties. Use an explicit key `(-priority, index)` with `min`.
10. **Dedup key.** `(date, description.strip(), Decimal)` works because `Decimal("-4.5") == Decimal("-4.50")` and they hash the same. `-0` equals `0`. Dedup runs before the month filter, and the warning is printed to stderr after the stdout write.
11. **Output buffering.** Build the entire output as a string, and write it only after loading, categorizing and formatting have all succeeded. This guarantees "no stdout on error".
12. **Table alignment.** Width is `max(len(header), max(len(cell)))`, using code-point `len`. Join cells with two spaces, then `rstrip()` each line. Right-aligned columns use `str.rjust`. East-Asian or combining characters are deliberately not width-aware.

## Constraints the spec must respect

- Flat `csvledger/` package at the repo root, with no `src/` directory. Standard library only, and pytest is for tests only. Run as `python -m csvledger` from the repo root.
- Load order is the rules file first, then the transaction files in argument order, and the first error wins.
- Stdout must stay empty on any error. The warning goes to stderr and comes after stdout.
- Error message formats are exact. `<path>` is the argv string as given. `<line>` is `csv.reader.line_num` after the record is read.
- Row check order is fixed (field count, date, amount for transactions; field count, category, type, pattern, priority, regex for rules). Header check order is also fixed (missing header, duplicate column, missing column).
- Exit 1 is never intentional. It is only a safety net for unexpected exceptions.
- Money formatting follows the contract: `quantize` with `ROUND_HALF_UP`, then `0.00` if the result is zero, otherwise `format(q, "f")`. Aggregates are summed unrounded.
- `-` is an ordinary filename and stdin is never read.
- JSON uses `indent=2` and `ensure_ascii=False`, ends with `\n`, and keeps the exact key order from the contract.

## Recommended module layout

```
csvledger/
  __init__.py     # empty
  __main__.py     # raise SystemExit(main())
  cli.py          # build_parser(), main(argv=None) -> int, top-level handler
  errors.py       # LedgerError(code, message); EXIT_* constants (USAGE=2, TX=3, RULES=4, INTERNAL=1)
  csvio.py        # read_records(path, required, err_code): UTF-8-sig read, header checks, yields (line, fields)
  transactions.py # parse_transactions(path) -> list[Transaction]
  rules.py        # parse_rules(path); Rule; categorize(tx, rules)
  dedup.py        # dedupe(rows) -> (kept, n_skipped)
  aggregate.py    # monthly_report(txs) -> sorted months and categories
  money.py        # fmt_money(); shared Decimal context
  render.py       # table(cols, rows), render_report/categorize in table and json
tests/
  conftest.py     # run_cli fixture; O1/O3/O4/O5 file writers
  test_cli.py, test_parsing.py, test_rules.py, test_dedup.py,
  test_money.py, test_render.py, test_golden.py
```

- `csvio` is shared by the transaction and rules parsers, with the error code and file kind passed in.
- `cli.main` does the following, in order:
  1. Parse arguments.
  2. Load the rules.
  3. Load the transactions.
  4. Dedup.
  5. Filter by month.
  6. Categorize.
  7. Aggregate.
  8. Render to a string.
  9. Write to stdout.
  10. Write the warning to stderr.
  11. Return 0.
- The exception handler maps `LedgerError` to `csvledger: error: {msg}` on stderr and returns its code. Any other `Exception` returns 1.

## Recommended test plan

| Case | In-process | Subprocess (bytes) |
|---|---|---|
| AC1: `--help` | exit 0, stdout mentions `report` and `categorize` | same |
| AC2: O1 table | `capsys` stdout equals the contract text exactly | compare exact bytes |
| AC3: O1 JSON | `json.loads`, check key order via `list(obj)`, January Groceries expenses `"-57.11"` | not needed |
| AC4: `categorize` on O1 | date order, `Blue Bottle Cafe` is `Coffee`, `-12.005` handled | not needed |
| AC5: `--month 2026-02` | only two rows, both `2026-02` | not needed |
| AC6: O4 | one Coffee row with count 1 and `-4.50`, stderr warning, exit 0 | check stderr text |
| AC7: O3 | exit 3, stdout empty, stderr equals the exact line | check stderr text |
| AC8: invalid regex | exit 4, message `invalid regex` | not needed |
| AC9: O5 | exact table including `0.13`, `-0.13`, `0.00`, `0.01` | not needed |
| AC10: determinism | not needed | run twice, assert equal bytes and `b"\r" not in out` (Windows CI guard) |

- Write golden files using `write_bytes` and `tmp_path`, so there is no CRLF translation. Pass relative paths with `cwd=tmp_path` so `<path>` in error messages matches the expectation.
- Add unit tests for the following:
  - **Money and rounding:** `-0.004` shows as `0.00`; `0.125` rounds to `0.13`; large values stay exact.
  - **Header errors:** duplicate and missing columns, an empty file (0 bytes), and a header-only file.
  - **Row errors:** field-count mismatch, blank-line skipping, and a multi-line quoted field for line numbers.
  - **Rules:** priority ties go to the earlier rule; zero rules gives `Uncategorized`.
  - **Dedup:** dedup runs across files before the `--month` filter, and `-4.5` equals `-4.50`.
  - **Usage errors:** bad `--month` (`2026-13`), bad `--format`, and missing `FILE` all give exit 2, with the last stderr line matching the contract regex.
  - **Exit-code safety net:** monkeypatch an internal function to raise `RuntimeError` and assert exit 1, no traceback, and one-line stderr.
  - **Robustness:** a directory passed as a file, an invalid UTF-8 byte, and a NUL byte (`csv.Error`) all map to the contract exit codes (3 or 4, depending on file kind).
  - **Unicode:** non-ASCII descriptions are aligned by code point.
  - **Hygiene:** assert `"Traceback" not in stderr` on every failure.

## Further recommendations

- Use `re.fullmatch` with `[0-9]` or `re.ASCII`, and state the choice explicitly in the spec (finding 8).
- Run all Decimal work inside a `localcontext` with a large `prec` (finding 7).
- Handle `csv.Error` as a file error (exit 3 or 4) and name the message format. Suggested wording: `<path>:<line>: malformed CSV`. The contract currently does not define it.
- Probe `reconfigure` on the target Pythons (3.11 and later) on Windows, and keep that test in the subprocess tier.

## Key findings

### Codebase state

1. **The repo is greenfield.** A glob shows only `brief.md`, `contract.md`, `.gitignore` and `.git/`. The one commit is `0b0d717 seed: brief and contract`. There is no code, no `docs/`, no config, no `pyproject.toml`, no `requirements*`, no `pytest.ini`, no `conftest.py`, no `tests/` and no `.gitattributes`. 2. **`.gitignore` contains only `__pycache__/`.** It does not cover `.pytest_cache/`.
3. **There are no integration surfaces to preserve.** The only conventions come from the contract:
   - a flat `csvledger/` package at the repo root, with no `src/`;
   - `python -m csvledger`, so a `csvledger/__main__.py` is needed;
   - pytest for tests only;
   - standard library only at runtime.
4. **The contract numbers its cases O1, O3, O4 and O5.** There is no O2, so the spec should say it is intentionally absent. AC5 uses O1 for the month filter.

### Pytest and layout gotchas

5. **A flat layout plus a `tests/` directory without `__init__.py` breaks a bare `pytest` run.** In pytest's default import mode only `tests/` goes on `sys.path`, not the repo root, so `import csvledger` fails.

   - Subprocess tests must pass `cwd=<repo root>`.
6. **Windows and git line endings.**
   - Fixtures must be written as bytes, or with `newline="\n"`. Otherwise `core.autocrlf` or the platform can turn `\n` into `\r\n`. The contract says "each line ends with `\n`".

7. **Exact arithmetic breaks above 28 digits.** The default `decimal` context has precision 28. Summing or quantizing amounts with more than 28 significant digits silently rounds, or raises `InvalidOperation`. That contradicts "sums are exact". The spec should require a dedicated `decimal.Context` with ample precision and traps enabled. Alternatively it could cap amount length, but the contract's regex has no cap.
8. **`\d` matches Unicode digits.** In Python 3 `str` patterns, `\d` accepts digits such as Arabic-Indic ones. `Decimal` and `int` accept them too. That affects:
   - the date regex;
   - the amount regex;
   - the priority regex;
   - the `--month` regex.

    - Duplicates inside a single file also count, and the same file passed twice duplicates everything.

11. **Month filter versus dedup order.**

    - The spec should say the filter runs after dedup.
    - An implementer who filters first would pass AC5 but fail the warning count.

4. **The contract numbers its cases O1, O3, O4 and O5.** There is no O2, so the spec should say it is intentionally absent. AC5 uses O1 for the month filter.

### Pytest and layout gotchas

5. **A flat layout plus a `tests/` directory without `__init__.py` breaks a bare `pytest` run.** In pytest's default import mode only `tests/` goes on `sys.path`, not the repo root, so `import csvledger` fails.
   - The fix is either a root `conftest.py` or a `pytest.ini`/`pyproject` setting of `pythonpath = .`. Pytest 7 or later supports that setting.
   - Subprocess tests must pass `cwd=<repo root>`.
6. **Windows and git line endings.**
   - Fixtures must be written as bytes, or with `newline="\n"`. Otherwise `core.autocrlf` or the platform can turn `\n` into `\r\n`. The contract says "each line ends with `\n`".
   - Text-mode `sys.stderr` on Windows translates `\n` to `\r\n`. The contract reconfigures only stdout.

### Contract ambiguities and edge cases

7. **Exact arithmetic breaks above 28 digits.** The default `decimal` context has precision 28. Summing or quantizing amounts with more than 28 significant digits silently rounds, or raises `InvalidOperation`. That contradicts "sums are exact". The spec should require a dedicated `decimal.Context` with ample precision and traps enabled. Alternatively it could cap amount length, but the contract's regex has no cap.
8. **`\d` matches Unicode digits.** In Python 3 `str` patterns, `\d` accepts digits such as Arabic-Indic ones. `Decimal` and `int` accept them too. That affects:
   - the date regex;
   - the amount regex;
   - the priority regex;
   - the `--month` regex.

   The spec should require `re.ASCII` or `[0-9]`, and `fullmatch`, because `$` also matches before a trailing newline. Without this, fullwidth digits are accepted, and the output then varies by input script.
9. **Priority and long digit strings.** `int()` on a string of more than 4300 digits raises `ValueError` in Python 3.11 or later. The spec should map this to "invalid priority" rather than let it reach exit 1.
10. **Dedup key is the parsed `Decimal` value.** `Decimal("-4.50") == Decimal("-4.5")` and the hashes are equal. `-0` equals `0`. The key is the raw, unrounded amount, so `-12.005` and `-12.01` are different keys.
    - The description is compared stripped, case-sensitively, with no inner whitespace collapse.
    - Duplicates inside a single file also count, and the same file passed twice duplicates everything.
    - O4 confirms the stripped description and numeric amount rules.
    - Two genuinely identical purchases on one day are collapsed by design. That is a product risk, not something the spec should change.
11. **Month filter versus dedup order.**
    - Duplicates share a date, so the filter cannot change which row survives.
    - The only observable effect is the warning count N, which includes duplicates outside the selected month.
    - The spec should say the filter runs after dedup.
    - An implementer who filters first would pass AC5 but fail the warning count.
12. **Rounding "once".**
    - Aggregates are summed raw, then rounded. Month totals are raw sums across categories. The displayed per-category values need not add up to the displayed month totals.
    - `-57.105` becomes `-57.11` under ROUND_HALF_UP (Decimal rounds half away from zero). O5 confirms `-0.125` becomes `-0.13`.
    - O5 is consistent: Misc income `0.125` gives `0.13`, expenses `-0.125` gives `-0.13`, and net `0` gives `0.00`.
    - Tiny income `0.010` gives `0.01`, expenses `-0.004` gives `0.00`, and net `0.006` gives `0.01`.
    - I checked O1 and O5 by hand and they match the contract.
13. **`-0.00` handling.** Test `q == 0` after quantizing. `Decimal("-0.00") == 0` is true, so it prints `0.00`. Do the check on the quantized value, not the raw one.
14. **Money fields in `categorize`.** "Formatted as money" implies the amount is rounded to 2 dp in both table and JSON. So `-12.005` shows as `-12.01` and `-0.004` as `0.00`. The JSON `amount` is implied to be rounded too, but the contract never says so explicitly. This should be stated.
15. **`line_num` with multiline quoted fields.**
    - `csv.reader.line_num` counts physical lines consumed, so an error on a record spanning lines 3 to 5 reports 5.
    - Blank lines still advance the count.
    - Do not use `text.splitlines()`. It also splits on `\x0b`, `\x0c`, `\x1c`, `\x85`, `\u2028` and similar, which corrupts both records and line numbers.
    - Use `io.StringIO(text, newline="")`, or open the file with `newline=""`.
16. **Decoding must be eager.** Text-mode file decoding is chunked. An invalid UTF-8 byte late in a file can surface after earlier row errors, which makes "first error wins" depend on buffer boundaries.
    - Read bytes, decode `utf-8-sig` fully, then parse.
    - This also yields the output-buffer behaviour needed for "stdout stays empty".
    - `utf-8-sig` strips only one leading BOM. A second BOM stays in the first header name, which then reports a missing column.
17. **"No header line" is under-specified.**
    - A 0-byte file gives zero records, so it is "missing header". A BOM-only file also gives zero records.
    - A file whose line 1 is blank gives a record `[]`. The contract says line 1 is the header but also says to skip blank rows. The most literal reading is that header `[]` leads to "missing column 'date'". The spec should state this explicitly.
    - A header with a trailing comma yields an empty-name column. Two of them give `duplicate column ''`.
18. **Field-count and csv.Error cases.**
    - `N` in "expected N fields" is the header's field count, including ignored extra columns.
    - A whitespace-only line yields one field, so it is a count mismatch, not a blank row.
    - `csv.Error` is not in the error table. Fields over the 131072-character limit raise it. Python 3.11 accepts NUL, I believe. An unterminated quote at EOF is accepted silently under default dialect settings. The spec should map `csv.Error` to a defined message and exit code.
19. **Header normalization.** Strip and lowercase (`.lower()`, not casefold). The reported duplicate `<name>` is the normalized form. Unicode `str.strip()` also strips NBSP and similar characters. The spec should say "Python `str.strip()`".
20. **AC10 conflicts with embedded newlines in the table.**
    - A quoted description containing `\r\n` or `\n` is preserved by `newline=""`.
    - In the `categorize` table the output would then contain `\r`, which violates "output contains no `\r`", and it breaks row alignment.
    - JSON escapes these characters, so it is fine.
    - The contract is silent on the table case. The spec must either define sanitization (for example, replace control characters and line breaks with a space) or declare the situation out of scope.
    - Sanitizing extends the contract, so flag it as a decision.
21. **Table width.** Width uses `len()` on code points, so CJK and combining characters misalign visually. That is accepted by the contract. The last column is right-stripped, so left-aligned `CATEGORY` and `DESCRIPTION` trailing pad disappears when they are last. Empty descriptions are allowed.
22. **Rules edge cases.**
    - `contains` uses `casefold()` on both sides. `regex` uses `re.search` with `IGNORECASE` against the stripped description.
    - A category literally named `Uncategorized` merges with the default bucket.
    - Categories differing only in case are distinct.
    - Priority comparison must be numeric, not string.
    - The ordering rule is: highest priority wins, ties go to file order.
    - `re.error` is the only exception named. Pathological patterns can still cause catastrophic backtracking, and no mitigation is required.
23. **Argparse behaviour to pin down.**
    - `prog="csvledger"` must be set explicitly. Otherwise `-m` gives `__main__.py`.
    - Subparsers are not required by default, so `python -m csvledger` with no command would not error. The spec should say it is exit 2 (`required=True`).
    - `--month` validation via a `type=` callable raising `ArgumentTypeError` produces `csvledger report: error: ...`. The contract's regex allows this form.
    - Abbreviations such as `--form` are accepted by default. Decide whether to disable them with `allow_abbrev=False`.
    - A repeated `--rules` means the last one wins unless specified.
    - A file named `-x` requires `--`.
    - In Python 3.14, argparse adds coloured help and error output controlled by `FORCE_COLOR` and `NO_COLOR`. ANSI codes could break the stderr regex. Pass `color=False` on 3.14 or later, or neutralize via the environment in tests.
    - Usage errors happen before any file is read, so exit 2 outranks 3 and 4.
24. **Stdout and stderr handling.**
    - Reconfigure `sys.stdout` in `main()`, not at import time.
    - Guard with `hasattr(sys.stdout, "reconfigure")`, because pytest's capture objects lack it.
    - Build the full output string and write it once, so errors leave stdout empty.
    - Write the duplicate warning after stdout, and flush in between.
    - Python's stderr uses `backslashreplace`, so error messages with non-ASCII values will not crash. Their bytes can still vary by console code page. Consider reconfiguring stderr to UTF-8 as well.
25. **Exit code 1 and tracebacks.** The brief says "never a traceback", while the contract says code 1 is "never intentional". The spec should require a top-level catch for unexpected exceptions. It should print `csvledger: error: internal error: ...` and exit 1. It should also handle `BrokenPipeError` explicitly.
26. **Year 0000.** `0000-01-01` matches the regex, but the date is invalid. `--month 0000-01` passes the regex and yields an empty result with exit 0.
27. **Path handling.**
    - `<path>` is the raw argv string, with Windows backslashes preserved.
    - Directories and permission errors map to "cannot read file". That is `OSError` on open, and `IsADirectoryError` on Windows is a `PermissionError`.
    - `-` is an ordinary filename, so stdin is never read.

## Constraints the spec must respect

- Python 3.11 or later, standard library only at runtime; pytest for tests only.
- A flat `csvledger/` package at the repo root, run as `python -m csvledger` from the repo root, with `prog="csvledger"`.
- Exit codes 0, 2, 3 and 4 as in the table. Code 1 is never intentional.
- Error lines on stderr have the exact form `csvledger: error: <msg>`. Stdout is empty on any error. Load order is rules first, then files in argument order, and the first error wins.
- The check orders in the contract are fixed.
  - Header checks run in the order: no header, duplicate column, missing column.
  - Row checks run in the order: field count, date, amount for transactions; field count, category, type, pattern, priority, regex for rules.
- Money is `Decimal` only. Aggregates are summed unrounded, then rounded once with ROUND_HALF_UP. `-0.00` is never printed. `net = income_raw + expenses_raw`.
- Dedup runs over all rows of all files before the `--month` filter, on the key (date, stripped description, numeric amount). The first occurrence is kept. The warning goes to stderr after stdout and only when N > 0.
- The JSON key order and the table column layout are exactly as shown. The sort order is month then category by code point for `report`, and date ascending with a stable input order for `categorize`.
- Output is UTF-8 with `\n` line endings and no locale use.
- The cases O1, O3, O4 and O5 are byte-exact oracles, and the acceptance tests must reproduce them.

## Recommendations

1. **Layout.** Specify the following files:
   - `csvledger/__init__.py` and `csvledger/__main__.py`, where `__main__` is `sys.exit(main())`;
   - modules for the CSV loader, rules, the money/decimal context, formatting and the CLI;
   - `tests/` with `test_*.py`;
   - a root `conftest.py` or `pytest.ini` with `pythonpath = .`;
   - a `.gitignore` addition for `.pytest_cache/`;
   - optionally `.gitattributes` with `* text=auto eol=lf` or a fixtures-specific rule.
2. **Define `main(argv=None) -> int`** so tests can run in-process. Also use subprocess tests with `cwd` set to the repo root for AC1, AC10 and byte-level checks, and compare raw bytes.
3. **Money module.** Use a dedicated `decimal.Context` with high precision and `traps=[InvalidOperation, Overflow]` rather than the default 28-digit context. Provide a single `fmt_money(value)` helper implementing the contract formula. Test the cases `-0`, `-0.00`, `-0.004`, `0.005` and `-12.005`, plus a long-digit sum.
4. **Parsing.**
   - Use `re.fullmatch` with `re.ASCII` for date, amount, priority and `--month`.
   - Read bytes, decode as `utf-8-sig`, and wrap in `io.StringIO(text, newline="")`.
   - Catch `OSError` for "cannot read file" and `UnicodeDecodeError` for "not valid UTF-8".
   - Decide the `csv.Error` mapping. I suggest exit 3 or 4 with a message such as `<path>:<line>: malformed CSV`.
   - Define explicitly what the header is when line 1 is blank.
5. **Resolve the open decisions in the spec**, flagged as open if the contract owner has not decided:
   - the `categorize` JSON `amount` is the rounded 2 dp string;
   - table sanitization of control characters and newlines (finding 20), with the spec stating whether this extends the contract;
   - the argparse abbreviation policy and `required=True` for subparsers;
   - reconfiguring stderr to UTF-8 and `newline="\n"`.
6. **Tests to require** beyond the acceptance criteria:
   - the month-filtered dedup warning count;
   - `--month` with duplicates outside the month;
   - multiline quoted field `line_num`;
   - BOM, duplicate or missing header, and 0-byte files;
   - invalid UTF-8 after a bad row, to prove decode-first ordering;
   - Unicode digits rejected;
   - rule priority ties and negative priority;
   - an empty report and an empty `categorize` for both formats;
